narration.full_text: Namaste students! Today, we're diving into the graphical method for solving linear equations. This visual approach helps us understand the nature of solutions. We'll learn how to plot lines and find their intersection points, which represent the solutions to our equations. Our learning goals for this section include explaining the graphical method, distinguishing between intersecting, parallel, and coincident lines, relating graphical outcomes to consistent, inconsistent, and dependent systems, and finally, solving pairs of linear equations by plotting graphs and identifying intersection points. Let's start by understanding how individual linear equations are represented graphically. A linear equation in two variables, like ax + by = c, always forms a straight line when plotted on a coordinate plane. For example, consider the equation x = 3. This represents a vertical line where every point on the line has an x-coordinate of 3, regardless of its y-coordinate. Similarly, the equation y = 2 represents a horizontal line where every point on the line has a y-coordinate of 2, regardless of its x-coordinate. When we plot these two lines, x=3 and y=2, on the same coordinate plane, they intersect at a single point. This intersection point is where both conditions are satisfied simultaneously. In this specific case, the lines x=3 and y=2 intersect at the point (3, 2). This point (3, 2) is the unique solution to the system of equations {x=3, y=2}. The coordinates of the intersection point give us the values of x and y that satisfy both equations.
